analysis.one_liner: Removes the Supreme Court's cap on punitive damages for victims of oil spills and maritime disasters.
analysis.headline: The bill to let juries award uncapped punitive damages against oil polluters was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2008 the Supreme Court ruled in Exxon Shipping v. Baker that punitive damages in maritime cases generally cannot exceed the compensatory damages awarded, a cap that sharply reduced what Exxon Valdez spill victims could collect. This bill would have written into federal law that punitive damages in maritime cases can be assessed without regard to compensatory damages, restoring the deterrence the cap removed. Introduced in May 2010 amid the BP Deepwater Horizon spill, it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which took no action on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People harmed by oil spills and other maritime disasters — fishermen, coastal residents, seafood workers, cleanup crews, and small businesses along affected waterways. If a company's reckless conduct destroys livelihoods, the bill would let juries award punitive damages sized to the wrongdoing rather than capped at the compensatory award, which is meant to punish and deter reckless conduct (the bill's own findings say so). Larger punitive exposure also gives oil shipping companies more reason to invest in safety up front.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil spill and maritime disaster victims

how_it_helps.text: The bill states that in a civil action for a maritime tort, punitive damages may be assessed without regard to the amount of compensatory damages, undoing the 1:1 ratio the Supreme Court imposed in Exxon Shipping v. Baker.

The bill's findings note that punitive damages punish reckless or worse behavior, deter future offenses, and compensate for intangible injuries that would otherwise go uncompensated, and that courts already have authority to reduce excessively large awards.

The bill's findings acknowledge the Supreme Court conceded that punitive awards have not been runaway verdicts and that the median punitive-to-compensatory ratio has remained below 1:1 — the basis for arguing the cap was not needed.

analysis.who_pays: Oil shipping companies, tanker owners, and other maritime operators, along with their insurers, would face larger and less predictable punitive-damage exposure after a disaster. Some of that cost would ultimately show up in shipping and fuel prices, and industry groups would argue that unpredictable liability raises the cost of maritime commerce.

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides a deliberate Supreme Court judgment. The Court's 1:1 ratio was designed to make maritime liability predictable, and the bill's own findings concede that median punitive-to-compensatory ratios have historically run below 1:1 — meaning the cap may rarely bind in typical cases and the practical change may be limited to rare catastrophic cases.
Uncapped punitive exposure could raise insurance costs and operating costs for shippers, some of which would be passed to consumers as slightly higher prices for transported goods and fuel.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but targeted: it matters most after a catastrophic spill like Exxon Valdez or Deepwater Horizon, exactly when deterrence is weakest under a 1:1 cap. The costs are higher liability and insurance costs for shippers, largely in rare cases, and the bill's own findings concede median award ratios were already below 1:1. The strongest objection is that Congress is overriding a carefully reasoned Supreme Court standard, though courts retain authority to trim excessive awards. On balance, the bill modestly shifted power toward spill victims and away from the shipping industry, at a cost concentrated in the industry itself.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee never scheduled a hearing or markup after the bill was referred to it, and the bill died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, joined by Sens. Robert Menendez and Patrick Leahy, introduced the Big Oil Polluter Pays Act on May 11, 2010, to remove the punitive-damage cap established in Exxon Shipping v. Baker.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day it was introduced.

That referral was the bill's last action of any kind; the committee took no further action and the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or floor consideration before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
The bill drew eight cosponsors — seven of 58 Senate Democrats and the Senate's one independent — all from one party and its allied independent, with no Republican cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil shipping companies, tanker owners, and their insurers are better off because the bill died: they keep the Supreme Court's 1:1 cap on punitive damages, which limits what oil spill victims can recover for intangible harm and keeps their disaster liability predictable. Nothing changed for spill victims, who remain subject to the cap the bill would have removed.

sides.party_line_note: The only sign of partisan shape is sponsorship: all 8 cosponsors were Democrats plus the Senate's sole independent, and no Republican cosponsored, but the bill never got a vote, so how the chamber would have split is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would have exposed them to uncapped punitive damages after maritime disasters like oil spills, the exact scenario the Exxon Shipping v. Baker cap shields them from. Their interest in keeping the cap runs against spill victims, who can currently recover no more than one dollar punitive for every compensatory dollar.

Unlimited punitive-damage exposure makes liability harder to price, raising premiums for their shipping clients. The savings would have come out of what victims could collect, not out of the insurers' customers in ordinary years.
Larger available punitive awards expand the value of maritime tort cases, which also means more resources for victims pursuing claims against polluters.
